key_insight: Chemical gradients in porous and crowded media can drive colloids and droplets via diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis, fundamentally altering transport, removal, breakthrough, and dispersion.
engineering_relevance: This matters for designing filters, soils, microfluidic systems, hydrogels, and biomedical environments where solute fronts can be leveraged to control particle migration and cleanup.
method: Review and synthesize the minimal physicochemical model for diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis.
Compare classic porous-media transport mechanisms with gradient-driven phoretic transport.
Summarize experiments in dead-end pores, flowing pathways, and micromodels across confined and living media.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports recent experimental results showing that diffuse solute fronts can enhance removal from dead-end pores and that cross-streamline migration can change macroscopic breakthrough and dispersion by orders of magnitude.
watch_item: Predictions may be highly geometry- and chemistry-dependent, especially when moving from 2D micromodels to 3D porous media where mixing can become chaotic.
paper_title: Diffusiophoretic transport of colloids and emulsions in complex environments
